body.text: LLMs learn from public data up to a cutoff date. Ask about your company's refund policy, last week's incident or a customer's contract, and the model has never seen it.
It will often answer anyway, confidently and wrongly. That's called a hallucination.
**Retrieval-Augmented Generation:** before the LLM answers, search your own documents for the most relevant pieces and add them to the prompt. The model answers from those pieces and can cite them.
Think of it as an open-book exam for the model.
A user asks: "Can contractors expense a home office chair?"

items: Search finds 3 paragraphs from the Expense Policy.
The prompt becomes: instructions + those 3 paragraphs + the question.
The LLM answers: "No. Contractors aren't covered for office furniture (Source: Expense Policy, section 4)."

body.text: Nothing was retrained. Update the policy document, and tomorrow's answer changes too.

slides.title: When RAG is the right tool

body.text: Use RAG when:

items: answers depend on private or company data
the data changes often (docs, tickets, prices)
users need sources they can check
different users are allowed to see different documents

body.text: Skip it when the model already knows enough (general coding questions), or when all the data fits easily in one prompt.

slides.title: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context

items: **Fine-tuning** teaches a model a style, format or skill. It's a poor way to add facts that change, because you'd retrain every time.
**Long context** pastes whole documents into the prompt. Fine for a few files, but slow and expensive for thousands, and details in the middle get missed.
**RAG** fetches only the relevant pieces at question time. Fresh, cheaper per question, and easy to trace back to sources.

body.text: Real systems often combine them.
An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector, often 384 to 3,072 of them) that represents what a piece of text means.
Texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, even with no words in common. "Reset my password" sits close to "I can't log in".
That's what lets search find meaning, not just matching words.
Two different models with two different jobs:

items: **Embedding model:** text in, vector out. Small, fast and cheap. Used to index documents and to encode each question.
**LLM:** text in, text out. Large, slower and more expensive. Used to write the final answer.

body.text: In RAG, the embedding model finds the right pieces. The LLM reads them and writes the answer.

slides.title: The two halves of every RAG system

items: **Offline (indexing):** collect documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk, and store the vectors plus metadata in a vector database. Runs ahead of time and again on every update.
**Online (answering):** embed the question, find the nearest chunks, build the prompt, call the LLM, and return the answer with citations. Runs on every question, usually in a second or two.
Support bots that answer from help-center articles
"Ask the wiki" assistants at work
Coding assistants that search your repo before suggesting code
Search engines that write a summary with links

body.text: If a chatbot shows its sources, there's a good chance RAG is behind it.

You now know what RAG is and when to use it. Next, you'll learn how each stage really works, and how interviewers test it, one topic at a time: from ingestion and chunking all the way to evaluation and safety.
By the end, you'll be able to design "ChatGPT for your company's docs" end to end, one of the most common AI system design interview questions.

questions.title: Why RAG
questions.prompt: What problem does RAG mainly solve?
options: LLMs don't know your private or recent data, so they guess
LLMs forget earlier turns in a long chat, so they lose track
LLMs answer too slowly, so search makes responses faster
LLMs can't follow formatting rules without extra examples
questions.keyIdea: RAG gives the model the facts it was never trained on.
questions.why: Without your documents in the prompt, the model fills gaps with plausible guesses.

ifWrong.1: That's conversation memory. RAG is about knowledge the model never had.
ifWrong.2: RAG adds a search step, so it usually adds a little latency.
ifWrong.3: Formatting is a prompting or fine-tuning job, not retrieval.

questions.title: Open book
questions.prompt: In a RAG system, what happens right before the LLM writes its answer?
options: Relevant pieces of your documents are retrieved and added to the prompt
The model is briefly fine-tuned on the matching documents
The whole document collection is pasted into the prompt
The question is matched to a cached answer from a past user
questions.keyIdea: Retrieve first, then generate.
questions.why: The model answers "open book" from the pieces it was handed.

ifWrong.1: Nothing is trained at question time. The pieces go into the prompt.
ifWrong.2: Only the top few relevant pieces fit and help. That's why we search.
ifWrong.3: A cache can sit in front of RAG, but RAG itself retrieves documents.

questions.title: Fresh docs
questions.prompt: Your expense policy changed this morning. What does a RAG system need so answers reflect the change?
options: Re-index the updated document
Increase the LLM's context window
Retrain the LLM on the new policy
Switch to a newer embedding model
questions.keyIdea: In RAG, fresh knowledge means fresh documents, not a new model.
questions.why: Re-indexing updates what search can find. The models stay the same.

ifWrong.1: A bigger window doesn't help if the new text never gets retrieved.
ifWrong.2: Retraining is slow and costly, and RAG exists so you don't have to.
ifWrong.3: The models are fine. The index still holds the old text.

questions.title: Fine-tune or RAG
questions.prompt: Which goal fits fine-tuning better than RAG?
options: Make the model always answer in your support team's tone and format
Answer questions about each customer's contract terms and renewal dates
Answer questions about this week's support tickets and their status
Cite the exact HR handbook section behind each answer
questions.keyIdea: Fine-tuning shapes behavior and style. RAG supplies facts.
questions.why: Tone and format are stable skills. Tickets, contracts and handbooks are changing facts that need sources.

ifWrong.1: Contracts are private facts that change. That's RAG.
ifWrong.2: Tickets change daily. Retrieval keeps up; fine-tuning can't.
ifWrong.3: Citations need the source text in the prompt. That's RAG.

questions.title: Two models
questions.prompt: Which statement about the embedding model and the LLM is true?
options: The embedding model turns text into a vector; the LLM writes the answer text
The LLM turns text into vectors; the embedding model writes the answer
Both are the same model, called in two different modes
The embedding model is the larger one, so it only runs at indexing time
questions.keyIdea: Embedding model finds, LLM writes.
questions.why: The embedding model maps text to vectors for search. The LLM reads the retrieved text and generates the reply.

ifWrong.1: Swapped. The embedding model makes vectors; the LLM writes.
ifWrong.2: They're usually separate models with different sizes and jobs.
ifWrong.3: It's usually smaller, and it also runs on every question.

questions.title: Meaning match
questions.prompt: "Reset my password" and "I can't log in" share no words. Why can vector search still match them?
options: Their embeddings are close because their meanings are similar
The search engine expands each query with a synonym list
An LLM rewrites every question before the search runs
Keyword search on word stems finds a shared root
questions.keyIdea: Embeddings capture meaning, not exact words.
questions.why: Similar meaning puts the two vectors close together, so search finds one from the other.

ifWrong.1: Synonym lists help keyword search. Vector search matches meaning directly.
ifWrong.2: Rewriting can help, but vector search matches these even without it.
ifWrong.3: They share no words or stems. Only meaning connects them.

questions.title: Count the vectors
questions.prompt: You index 1,000 documents, about 12 chunks each. How many embeddings do you store?
questions.keyIdea: You embed every chunk, not every document.
questions.why: 1,000 documents x 12 chunks = 12,000 vectors.

ifWrong.1: That's one per document, but search works on chunks.
ifWrong.2: Multiply, don't add. Each of the 1,000 documents has 12 chunks.

questions.title: Every question
questions.prompt: Which work happens on every user question, not ahead of time?
options: Embed the question, search for nearby chunks, then call the LLM
Re-embed the documents that match the question, then search
Split the matching documents into chunks, then call the LLM
Rebuild the vector index for the user's documents, then search
questions.keyIdea: Indexing happens offline; answering happens online.
questions.why: Chunking and embedding documents is done ahead of time, so each question only needs one embedding, one search and one LLM call.

ifWrong.1: Documents are embedded once, offline. Only the question is embedded live.
ifWrong.2: Chunking happens offline, before any question arrives.
ifWrong.3: The index is built ahead of time and updated when documents change.

body.text: A RAG system can only answer from what it retrieves, and it can only retrieve what ingestion stored.
If a table was mangled, a page was skipped, or a chunk cut a fact in half, no reranker or prompt can fix it later. Many "the model got it wrong" bugs in RAG are really ingestion bugs.
Raw documents go through the same steps every time:

items: **Connect:** pull from sources like wikis, drives, tickets and chat.
**Parse:** turn files into clean text and structure.
**Clean:** strip boilerplate and remove duplicates.
**Chunk:** split text into pieces search can return.
**Enrich:** attach metadata to every chunk.
**Embed and index:** store vectors plus metadata.

body.text: Search returns chunks, not whole documents, so every step shapes what the model sees.

items: **PDFs:** multi-column layouts, headers and footers repeated on every page, tables drawn as lines. Use a layout-aware parser.
**Scanned PDFs and images:** need OCR first. OCR mistakes turn into search misses, so check the quality.
**HTML:** strip menus, ads and cookie banners. Keep headings and lists.
**Slides and spreadsheets:** keep the slide title or column headers with each piece of content.

body.text: Rule of thumb: read the parsed text of 20 real documents before you tune anything else.
Real document sets are full of repeats: the same policy copied into five wikis, email threads quoting each other, old and new versions side by side.
Duplicates waste context tokens and push other useful results out of the top results.

items: Remove exact duplicates with a content hash.
Remove near-duplicates with a similarity check (for example MinHash).
Drop boilerplate such as repeated legal footers.
Decide early whether personal data must be removed before indexing.

body.text: Three reasons:

items: Embedding models have an input limit, often 512 to 8,000 tokens.
One vector for a whole long document blurs many ideas into one point.
The LLM's context window is a budget. You want to send only the relevant parts.

body.text: Chunking gives each idea its own vector, so search can return just the paragraphs that matter.

items: **Too big:** the vector averages many topics, so matches get weak and tokens are wasted.
**Too small:** a chunk loses the context it needs. "It increased by 20%" means nothing without knowing what "it" is.

body.text: A common starting point is 200 to 500 tokens with 10 to 20% overlap. Overlap makes a sentence near a boundary appear whole in at least one chunk.
These are starting numbers. Pick the final size by measuring recall@k on real questions.

items: **Fixed size:** split every N tokens. Simple and fast, but cuts sentences and tables.
**Sentence or paragraph:** split on natural boundaries. Better meaning, uneven sizes.
**Recursive:** try headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, until pieces fit the size limit. A strong default.
**Structure-aware:** follow the document's own sections, tables and code blocks.
**Semantic:** split where the topic changes, using embedding similarity between sentences. Best boundaries, most compute.
Keep each table with its header row, or turn each row into a sentence: "Plan Pro costs $49 for 10 seats."
Keep code blocks whole. Half a function is useless.
Keep list items with the sentence that introduces them.

Add the heading path to each chunk, like "HR Handbook > Leave > Parental leave", so the chunk still makes sense on its own. This is often called a contextual header, and it usually improves retrieval.

body.text: Small chunks match precisely. Big sections give the model enough context. You can have both:

items: Index small chunks (for example 150 tokens).
When one matches, send its parent section (for example 1,000 tokens) to the LLM.

body.text: A lighter version is the sentence window: match one sentence, then send the few sentences around it.
Store with each chunk: document ID, title, source URL, section path, author, created and updated times, version, language and access permissions.

items: **Filters** use it: "only 2026 docs", "only the billing product".
**Citations** use it: "Source: HR Handbook, updated Mar 2026."
**Freshness** uses it: prefer the newest version.
**Security** uses it: only return chunks the user is allowed to see.

body.text: The vector is only for matching. Anything you want to show or filter on must be stored next to it.

items: Prefer change feeds or webhooks from the source over full re-crawls. Poll only when nothing else exists.
Track every chunk by document ID and a content hash. On an edit, re-embed only the chunks whose hash changed.
Replace a document's old chunks in one step (an upsert), so stale text never lingers next to new text.
Keep document versions, so you can tell old from new and roll back.

body.text: A deleted document must disappear from search quickly. Process delete events by document ID and remove all of its chunks.
Permission changes matter just as much. If someone loses access to a document, their searches must stop returning its chunks.
Events get missed, so run a regular reconciliation job that compares the index with the source and fixes any drift.
When asked "How would you ingest the data?", cover these in about a minute:

items: Sources, connectors, and how you detect changes
Parsing per format, especially PDFs and tables
Chunking strategy and size, and how you'd tune it with recall@k
Metadata, including permissions
Updates, deletes and reconciliation

body.text: Bringing up deletes and permissions before you're asked is a strong Senior signal.

questions.title: Big chunks
questions.prompt: Why do very large chunks hurt retrieval?
options: One embedding averages many topics, so the match is diluted
Vector databases reject chunks over a few hundred tokens
Bigger chunks need more embedding dimensions to fit
The LLM can only read chunks shorter than 1,000 tokens
questions.keyIdea: One vector per chunk. The more ideas in a chunk, the blurrier its vector.
questions.why: Large chunks mix topics, so similarity to any one question drops, and they waste context tokens.

ifWrong.1: Vector stores hold fixed-size vectors. Chunk length doesn't change that.
ifWrong.2: The model's vector size is fixed. A long chunk gets the same number of dimensions.
ifWrong.3: LLMs read far more than that. The real issue is the blurry vector.

questions.title: Cut sentences
questions.prompt: You split every 300 tokens with no overlap, and a key sentence is cut in half. Best fix?
options: Add 10 to 20% overlap, or split on sentence boundaries
Switch to an embedding model with more dimensions
Double the chunk size to 600 tokens so cuts happen less often
Strip stop words so each sentence fits inside one chunk
questions.keyIdea: Overlap and sentence-aware splits keep ideas whole.
questions.why: Neither half of a split sentence carries the full meaning. Overlap repeats the boundary text in both chunks.

ifWrong.1: More dimensions can't rebuild a sentence that was cut in half.
ifWrong.2: Bigger chunks still cut sentences somewhere, and they blur the vector.
ifWrong.3: Removing words damages meaning and doesn't stop the cut.

questions.title: Split tables
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: Markdown docs are cut every 500 tokens, splitting a pricing table in the middle.
options: Rows lose their header row, so answers about the table come out wrong
500 tokens is too small a chunk size for Markdown files
Embedding models can't read Markdown table syntax, so tables are ignored
The table should be removed, since tables don't embed well
questions.keyIdea: Keep tables with their headers.
questions.why: A row like "Pro | 49 | 10" means nothing without "Plan | Price | Seats".

ifWrong.1: Size isn't the problem. Any fixed cut can split a table.
ifWrong.2: They can read it. The trouble is the rows that lost their header.
ifWrong.3: Tables hold key facts. Keep them with headers, or turn rows into sentences.

questions.title: Citation metadata
questions.prompt: Which metadata lets the answer show "Source: HR Handbook, updated Mar 2026"?
options: Title, source and updated timestamp
The chunk's embedding vector
The chunk's overlap and token count
The similarity score from the search
questions.keyIdea: Citations and freshness come from metadata, not from the vector.
questions.why: The vector is only for matching. Display info must be stored alongside it.

ifWrong.1: A vector is just numbers for matching. It can't be turned back into a title.
ifWrong.2: Those describe chunking, not where the text came from.
ifWrong.3: The score says how well it matched, not where it came from.

questions.title: Chunk count
questions.prompt: 2M documents, about 4,000 tokens each, 500-token chunks with 100-token overlap. About how many chunks?
options: 2M
questions.keyIdea: Chunks per doc is roughly doc tokens divided by (chunk size minus overlap).
questions.why: Each new chunk moves forward 400 tokens, so 4,000 / 400 = 10 chunks per doc, and 2M x 10 = 20M.

ifWrong.1: That forgets the overlap: 4,000 / 500 = 8.
ifWrong.2: That's one chunk per document.
ifWrong.3: That's 100 chunks per document. Each chunk adds 400 new tokens, so it's 10.

questions.title: Stale chunks
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: when a document is edited, its new chunks are added but its old chunks stay in the index.
options: Old text still gets retrieved; replace a document's chunks by its ID
The embedding model must be retrained after every document edit to stay accurate
Edits should be ignored until a monthly full re-index
Overlap between old and new chunks causes duplicate vectors
questions.keyIdea: Updates must replace, not just add.
questions.why: Old chunks still match questions and return stale or conflicting answers.

ifWrong.1: The model is fine. The index still holds the old chunks.
ifWrong.2: That serves stale answers for weeks. Replace chunks on each edit.
ifWrong.3: Overlap isn't the cause. The old chunks were never removed.

questions.title: Changed chunks
questions.prompt: 100K documents are edited per day, 10 chunks each, and about 2 chunks actually change per edit. With chunk hashes, how many chunks do you re-embed daily?
options: 1M
2M
questions.keyIdea: Hash chunks and re-embed only what changed.
questions.why: 100K edits x 2 changed chunks = 200K.

ifWrong.1: That re-embeds every chunk of every edited document.
ifWrong.2: That's one chunk per edit. About 2 change each time.
ifWrong.3: That's 20 chunks per edit. Only about 2 change.

body.text: An embedding model turns text into a fixed-length list of numbers, for example 768 or 1,536 of them. Texts with similar meaning land close together.

items: The length is set by the model, whether the input is 5 words or 500.
Every model has its own space. A vector from model A can't be compared with one from model B.
Retrieval can never be better than the embedding model. If it can't tell two meanings apart, no index can.
**Cosine similarity:** the angle between two vectors, from -1 to 1. Length doesn't matter.
**Dot product:** angle times length. Ranks the same as cosine when vectors are normalized to length 1.
**Euclidean (L2) distance:** straight-line distance. For normalized vectors, it also ranks the same as cosine.

body.text: Use the metric the model was trained for. Most text models are used with normalized vectors and cosine or dot product.
The query and each document are encoded separately. Document vectors are computed once, at indexing time, and stored.
At question time you only:

items: Embed the query (one fast model call).
Compare it with the stored vectors.

body.text: The catch: the model never reads the query and the document together, so it misses fine details. Topic 4 (re-ranking) fixes that for the top results.
Judge models on your own data, not only on a public leaderboard like MTEB:

items: **Quality:** recall@k on 100 to 200 real questions with known right chunks.
**Domain and language:** legal, code, medical or multilingual text may need a specialized model.
**Max input length:** longer chunks get truncated or rejected.
**Dimensions:** more dimensions mean more memory and slower search.
**Cost and hosting:** an API priced per token, or self-hosted. Some data can't leave your network.

body.text: Raw vector memory = number of vectors x dimensions x bytes per number.

items: float32 = 4 bytes, float16 = 2, int8 = 1, binary = 1/8.
Example: 10M chunks x 1,024 dimensions x 4 bytes = about 41 GB.

body.text: The index adds more on top, for example the links in an HNSW graph.
Some models let you keep only the first part of each vector (Matryoshka embeddings), for example 256 of 1,024 dimensions, for a small recall cost.

items: **float16:** half the memory, almost no recall loss.
**int8:** a quarter of the memory, a small recall loss.
**Product quantization (PQ):** splits each vector into pieces and stores a short code per piece. Often 30x smaller or more, with more recall loss.
**Binary:** 1 bit per dimension, 32x smaller. Use it only with re-scoring.

body.text: The common pattern: search the small vectors for the top 100 candidates, then re-score those with full-precision vectors. You keep most of the recall for a fraction of the memory.
Exact search compares the query with every vector. It's perfect, and fine for small collections, but too slow at 100M vectors.
Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes check only a small part of the data and still find most true neighbors.

items: **Recall@10 = 95%** means the index found, on average, 9.5 of the true top 10.
Every ANN index trades **recall, latency and memory**. You tune for two; you pay with the third.

body.text: HNSW stacks layers of graphs: a few long links at the top, dense links at the bottom. A search starts at the top, walks toward the query, and drops down a layer at a time.

items: **M:** links per node. Higher means better recall and more memory.
**efSearch:** candidates explored per query. Higher means better recall and more latency.
**efConstruction:** build effort. Higher means a better graph and a slower build.

body.text: Strengths: high recall at low latency, easy inserts. Weaknesses: the graph lives in memory, and deletes are usually only marked, then cleaned up later.
IVF groups vectors into clusters with k-means, for example 4,096 clusters. Each vector goes into the list of its nearest cluster center.
At question time, it finds the closest few centers and scans only their lists.

items: **nlist:** number of clusters. More clusters means shorter lists to scan.
**nprobe:** clusters scanned per query. Higher means better recall and more latency.

body.text: IVF uses less memory than HNSW and pairs well with PQ (IVF-PQ) for billion-scale sets. Its weakness: a true neighbor in a cluster you didn't scan is missed.

items: **A library (FAISS, hnswlib):** fastest, but you build storage, updates, filters and scaling yourself.
**Postgres with pgvector:** vectors next to your data, with SQL filters and transactions. Great when you already run Postgres and the data fits on one machine.
**A vector database (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus):** built-in sharding, filtering and managed scaling.
**A search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch):** strong keyword search plus vector search in one place, which helps hybrid retrieval (Topic 3).

body.text: Interview tip: state the needs first (scale, filters, update rate, latency, team skills), then pick a tool.
Real queries almost always need filters: customer, permissions, product, date.

items: **Post-filtering:** take the top k, then drop what doesn't match. A strict filter can leave few or zero results.
**Filtered search:** apply the filter during the search, so all k results pass it. Most vector stores support this.
**Partition by tenant:** a separate index or namespace per customer. Strong isolation and easy deletes, but many small indexes to run.

body.text: Permissions belong in the search itself, never only in the prompt.
A new model means a new vector space. Every document must be re-embedded; you can't mix old and new vectors.
A safe migration:

items: Build a second index with the new model in the background.
Write new and changed documents to both indexes.
Compare both on the same question set.
Switch reads with a flag, keep the old index for rollback, then delete it.

body.text: Store the model name and version with every vector, so a mismatch is caught early.
When asked "How would you store and search the vectors?", cover:

items: The embedding model and how you'd test it on your data
Vector count, dimensions and the memory math
The index type and its recall versus latency knobs
Filters and permissions inside the search
How you'd re-embed when the model changes

body.text: Doing the memory math out loud ("10M x 1,024 x 4 bytes is about 41 GB, so int8 gets us to about 10 GB") is a strong Senior signal.

questions.title: Fast search
questions.prompt: Why is bi-encoder retrieval fast enough for millions of documents?
options: Document vectors are precomputed, so only the query is embedded live
The model reads the query together with each document in a single pass
Documents are matched by keyword first, then embedded on the fly
Vectors are compressed so tightly that comparisons cost nothing
questions.keyIdea: Precompute document vectors once; only the query is encoded at search time.
questions.why: Comparing vectors is cheap. Running a model on every document per query is not.

ifWrong.1: That's a cross-encoder. It's accurate but far too slow for millions of documents.
ifWrong.2: Only the query is embedded at search time. Document vectors already exist.
ifWrong.3: Compression saves memory. The speed comes from precomputing document vectors.

questions.title: Cosine score
questions.prompt: Two embeddings have a cosine similarity of 0.92. What does that tell you?
options: The model places the two texts very close in meaning
About 92% of the words in the two texts are the same
An answer built from them is 92% likely to be correct
The two documents are 92% of the way to being identical
questions.keyIdea: Cosine measures the angle between meanings, not word overlap or correctness.
questions.why: Two texts with different words can score high if they mean the same thing.

ifWrong.1: Cosine compares vector directions. Texts can score high with no shared words.
ifWrong.2: Similarity says the texts are related, not that an answer is right.
ifWrong.3: Cosine isn't a percentage of sameness. It reflects a small angle between vectors.

questions.title: Float32 memory
questions.prompt: 10M chunks, 1,024 dimensions, stored as float32. About how much raw vector memory?
options: 41 GB
10 GB
82 GB
4 GB
questions.keyIdea: Size = vectors x dimensions x bytes per number.
questions.why: 10M x 1,024 x 4 bytes = about 41 GB.

ifWrong.1: That forgets the 4 bytes per float32 number.
ifWrong.2: That uses 8 bytes per number. float32 is 4 bytes.
ifWrong.3: Check the zeros: 10M x 1,024 is about 10 billion numbers.

questions.title: Int8 memory
questions.prompt: The same 10M x 1,024 vectors stored as int8 instead of float32. About how much memory?
options: 10 GB
41 GB
20 GB
5 GB
questions.keyIdea: int8 uses 1 byte per number, a quarter of float32.
questions.why: 10M x 1,024 x 1 byte = about 10 GB.

ifWrong.1: That's still float32 at 4 bytes per number.
ifWrong.2: That's float16 at 2 bytes per number.
ifWrong.3: int8 is 1 byte per number, not half a byte.

questions.title: HNSW vs IVF
questions.prompt: Which statement about HNSW and IVF is true?
options: HNSW usually gives high recall at low latency but needs more memory
IVF compares each query with every vector, which is why recall is high
HNSW returns exact results, so its recall is always a perfect 100%
IVF has no tuning knobs, so its recall is fixed when the index is built
questions.keyIdea: Every ANN index trades recall, speed and memory.
questions.why: HNSW keeps a graph in memory. IVF scans only nearby clusters and is tuned with nprobe.

ifWrong.1: IVF scans only the nprobe nearest clusters. That's why it's fast.
ifWrong.2: HNSW is approximate. It can miss true neighbors; efSearch trades recall for speed.
ifWrong.3: nprobe is IVF's main knob. Raise it for recall, lower it for speed.

questions.title: Model mismatch
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: queries now use a new embedding model, but the document vectors were made with the old one.
options: The vectors live in different spaces; re-embed the documents
It only adds some latency until the query cache warms up
The query cache needs clearing, but the index itself is fine
The LLM will notice the mismatch and correct the final answer
questions.keyIdea: Queries and documents must share one embedding model.
questions.why: Each model has its own vector space. Mixing them gives close to random results.

ifWrong.1: Speed isn't the problem. The similarity scores become close to random.
ifWrong.2: The index is the problem. Its vectors came from the old model.
ifWrong.3: The LLM only sees what retrieval returns. Bad retrieval means bad context.

questions.title: IVF recall
questions.prompt: Your IVF index finds only 8 of the true top 10 (compared with exact search). Which knob helps most?
options: Raise nprobe so each query scans more clusters
Lower the dimensions so the search runs faster
Shorten the chunks so each vector is more precise
Raise the LLM temperature for more varied answers
questions.keyIdea: nprobe is IVF's recall versus speed dial.
questions.why: Scanning more clusters finds more true neighbors, at the cost of more comparisons.

ifWrong.1: Fewer dimensions loses information. It won't help IVF find the missed neighbors.
ifWrong.2: Chunk size changes what's indexed, not how well IVF finds the true neighbors.
ifWrong.3: Temperature affects generation, not retrieval.

questions.title: Filter after search
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: search returns the top 10 chunks, then removes the ones the user can't access. Some users get zero results.
options: A filter after search can drop all 10; filter during the search
The embedding model doesn't understand permissions; retrain it
Ten is too few; always fetch the top 1,000 and filter after that
Users with zero results should get a cached answer from other users
questions.keyIdea: Apply filters inside the search, not after it.
questions.why: When most chunks are off-limits, the top 10 can all be filtered out. Filtered search returns 10 allowed results.

ifWrong.1: Models don't do access control. Permissions are metadata filters.
ifWrong.2: Fetching more helps a little but still fails for strict filters, and it costs latency.
ifWrong.3: That hides the bug and can leak content the user isn't allowed to see.

questions.title: Re-embedding cost
questions.prompt: You switch embedding models and must re-embed 20M chunks of about 400 tokens each. At $0.02 per million tokens, about how much does it cost?
questions.keyIdea: Re-embedding is usually cheap in API cost. Time, rate limits and running two indexes are the real cost.
questions.why: 20M x 400 = 8 billion tokens = 8,000 million tokens x $0.02 = $160.

ifWrong.1: Check the zeros: 8 billion tokens is 8,000 million, not 800 million.
ifWrong.2: That uses $0.20 per million tokens.
ifWrong.3: That prices per thousand tokens. The rate is per million.

questions.title: Binary vectors
questions.prompt: You switch to 1-bit binary vectors to save memory, and recall drops. What's the standard fix?
options: Fetch about 100 candidates, then re-score them at full precision
Go back to float32 for every vector, since binary can never work well
Add more dimensions to the binary vectors so they hold more detail
Return only the top 3 results so that fewer mistakes are visible
questions.keyIdea: Search small, re-score precise.
questions.why: Binary search is a cheap first pass. Re-scoring 100 candidates with full vectors recovers most of the lost recall.

ifWrong.1: That gives up the 32x memory saving. Re-scoring keeps both.
ifWrong.2: The model sets the dimensions. Re-scoring is the usual fix.
ifWrong.3: That hides the problem and lowers recall even more.

body.text: If the right chunk isn't in the top results, the LLM can't use it. Retrieval quality caps answer quality.
Measure retrieval on its own:

items: **Recall@k:** how often a right chunk shows up in the top k.
**MRR:** how high the first right chunk ranks, on average.

body.text: Build a test set of 100 to 200 real questions with their right chunks before you tune anything. Topic 7 goes deeper on evaluation.
Dense search embeds the query and finds the nearest chunk vectors.
Good at:

items: Paraphrases and synonyms: "get my money back" finds "Refund policy".
Natural-language questions.

body.text: Weak at:

items: Exact strings: IDs, error codes, SKUs, rare names.
Negation: "not covered" can sit close to "covered".
Very short queries that carry little meaning.

body.text: BM25 scores a chunk by the query words it contains:

items: Rare words count more than common ones. "ERR_4012" matters more than "the".
Repeating a word helps, but less each time.
Long chunks are normalized, so they don't win just by being long.

body.text: Good at exact terms, codes, names and acronyms. Weak at synonyms. It's cheap, fast and needs no model.
Learned sparse models such as SPLADE add related words to each chunk, which closes part of the synonym gap.
Run keyword and dense search in parallel and merge the two lists. Each catches what the other misses, so hybrid usually beats either one alone.
Two ways to merge:

items: **Score blending:** normalize both scores, then weight them, for example 0.7 dense + 0.3 keyword. Needs tuning, because the scales differ.
**Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF):** uses ranks only. Simple, robust and a strong default.

body.text: Each document gets 1 / (k + rank) from every list it appears in. k is often 60.
With k = 60:

items: **Doc A:** rank 1 in keyword, rank 2 in dense: 1/61 + 1/62 = about 0.0325
**Doc B:** rank 3 in keyword, rank 1 in dense: 1/63 + 1/61 = about 0.0323
**Doc C:** rank 2 in keyword only: 1/62 = about 0.0161

body.text: Showing up in both lists beats ranking high in just one.
Users type messy queries. Fix them before you search:

items: **Standalone rewrite:** in a chat, turn "what about contractors?" into "PTO policy for contractors", using the conversation.
**Clean up:** fix typos, expand acronyms ("PTO" to "paid time off"), drop filler words.
**HyDE:** ask an LLM to write a short fake answer, then embed that. A fake answer often looks more like the real document than the question does.

body.text: Each rewrite is an extra LLM call, often a few hundred ms. Use a small, fast model.

items: **Multi-query:** write 3 to 5 versions of the question, search each, merge with RRF. Better recall for vague questions.
**Decomposition:** split a compound question into parts. "Compare the 2025 and 2026 parental leave policies" becomes one search per year.

body.text: Run the searches in parallel. Added latency is the rewrite call plus the slowest search, not the sum of all searches.
Metadata turns "similar" into "relevant right now":

items: **Hard filters:** product = billing, language = en, user can access. Apply them inside the search (Topic 2).
**Soft boosts:** rank newer or more trusted documents higher without hiding the rest.
**Filters from the question:** "2026 pricing" becomes year = 2026, using rules or a small LLM call.

body.text: Old and new versions of a page look almost the same to an embedding. Only metadata can tell them apart.
Retrieve wide, then narrow:

items: Fetch 50 to 100 candidates.
Re-rank them (Topic 4).
Send the best 5 to 10 to the LLM.

body.text: Too few, and the right chunk sits just past the cutoff. Too many, and you pay for more tokens while the model misses facts buried in the middle of a long context.
Be careful with fixed score cutoffs. Scores aren't comparable across queries, so a fixed threshold can drop good results.
Real systems have several sources: docs, tickets, code, a SQL database.

items: A router (rules or a small LLM) picks which sources to search, or whether to search at all.
"What's our refund policy?" goes to the docs index.
"How many refunds did we issue last week?" goes to SQL. Vector search can't count.

body.text: Searching every source every time adds latency and noise.
When an answer is wrong, check retrieval first:

items: Is the right chunk in the index at all? If not, it's an ingestion bug (Topic 1).
Is it in the top 100? If not, try hybrid search or query rewriting.
In the top 100 but not the top 5? It's a ranking problem. Add re-ranking (Topic 4).
In the prompt, but the answer is still wrong? It's a generation problem (Topic 6).

body.text: Log the query, the retrieved IDs and their scores for every request, so you can replay failures.
When asked "How would you retrieve the right context?", cover:

items: Hybrid search (BM25 plus dense), merged with RRF
Query rewriting for chat follow-ups
Filters for permissions, product and freshness, inside the search
Retrieve wide (50 to 100), re-rank, send the best few
Recall@k on a labeled question set to prove it works

body.text: Explaining why dense search alone misses error codes and IDs is a strong Senior signal.

questions.title: Error codes
questions.prompt: A user searches "ERR_4012 timeout" and dense-only search misses the doc that mentions ERR_4012. Why?
options: Embeddings blur rare exact strings like codes; add keyword search
The embedding dimension is too small to store a code like that one
The chunk overlap pushed the error code into a neighboring chunk
The query is too short, so it must be expanded into 5 variants first
questions.keyIdea: Keyword search catches exact strings that vectors blur.
questions.why: Embeddings capture meaning. "ERR_4012" carries little meaning, but it's an exact match for BM25.

ifWrong.1: More dimensions won't help. A code has little meaning for the model to capture.
ifWrong.2: Overlap repeats text; it doesn't hide it. The miss comes from the search method.
ifWrong.3: Expansion adds cost and noise. An exact keyword match finds it directly.

questions.title: Meaning match
questions.prompt: Which search is dense retrieval better at than keyword search?
options: "how do I get my money back" finding a doc titled "Refund policy"
"SKU-88213" finding the product page that lists that exact SKU
"RFC 7231" finding the spec that has that number in its title
"ERR_4012" finding the runbook that lists that exact error code
questions.keyIdea: Dense search matches meaning even with no shared words.
questions.why: "money back" and "refund" share no words but mean the same thing.

ifWrong.1: Exact IDs are where keyword search is strongest.
ifWrong.2: An exact number in a title is a keyword match.
ifWrong.3: Rare codes are where keyword search beats dense search.

questions.title: RRF score
questions.prompt: With RRF and k = 60, a document is rank 1 in keyword search and rank 3 in dense search. What's its fused score?
options: About 0.032
About 0.016
About 1.33
About 0.0003
questions.keyIdea: RRF adds 1 / (k + rank) from each list.

ifWrong.1: That counts only one list.
ifWrong.2: That forgets k: 1/1 + 1/3.
ifWrong.3: That multiplies the two parts. RRF adds them.

questions.title: Follow-up queries
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: in a chat, the user's follow-up is "what about contractors?", and retrieval searches just that text.
options: The query lacks context; rewrite it into a standalone question
Contractors should be filtered out of the index for privacy reasons
The chunks are too large to match such a short, specific question
A reranker would fix this without any change to the query itself
questions.keyIdea: Rewrite follow-ups into standalone queries before searching.
questions.why: "what about contractors?" alone matches almost anything. "PTO policy for contractors" matches the right doc.

ifWrong.1: That hides the very documents the user is asking about.
ifWrong.2: Chunk size isn't the problem. The query is missing "PTO policy".
ifWrong.3: A reranker only reorders what search found, and search used the wrong query.

questions.title: Multi-query cost
questions.prompt: What's the main trade-off of multi-query expansion?
options: Better recall, but extra latency and cost per question
Better precision, but it usually lowers recall for vague questions
Lower cost per question, but answers get noticeably worse
It replaces the reranker, so the pipeline gets simpler
questions.keyIdea: More searches find more, but each one costs time and money.
questions.why: You add an LLM call to write the variants, plus several searches to run and merge.

ifWrong.1: More queries usually raise recall. The extra results can add noise.
ifWrong.2: It costs more: an LLM call plus several searches.
ifWrong.3: Merging more results makes good ranking matter even more.

questions.title: Old pricing
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: a user asks about 2026 pricing, and the 2023 pricing page ranks first.
options: Ranking ignores dates; filter or boost by date and version
The embedding model is broken and needs to be replaced
The chunks are too small to include the year in the text
The LLM temperature is too high, so it picks older facts
questions.keyIdea: Use metadata to keep results current.
questions.why: Old and new pricing pages look almost the same to an embedding. Only date or version metadata separates them.

ifWrong.1: The model works. Any embedding model sees the two pages as near twins.
ifWrong.2: Even with the year in the text, the vectors stay close. Use metadata.
ifWrong.3: Temperature affects wording, not which page search ranks first.

questions.title: Multi-query latency
questions.prompt: Multi-query: an LLM rewrite takes 300 ms, then 4 searches of 40 ms each run in parallel, then merging takes 10 ms. How much latency does this add compared with one 40 ms search?
options: About 310 ms
About 430 ms
About 120 ms
About 350 ms
questions.keyIdea: Parallel searches cost the slowest one, not the sum.
questions.why: 300 + 40 + 10 = 350 ms in total, versus 40 ms before, so about 310 ms more.

ifWrong.1: That runs the 4 searches one after another.
ifWrong.2: That counts only the extra searches and forgets the 300 ms rewrite.
ifWrong.3: That's the total. The question asks how much it adds to the 40 ms search.

questions.title: Too much context
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: to be safe, the system sends the top 50 retrieved chunks straight into the prompt.
options: It wastes tokens and buries key facts; re-rank and send the best few
Fifty is too few; send the top 200 so that nothing ever gets missed
The LLM can't accept more than 10 chunks at once, so the request fails
No flaw: more context always makes the final answer more accurate
questions.keyIdea: Retrieve wide, re-rank, send few.
questions.why: Every chunk costs tokens, and models miss facts buried in long, noisy context.

ifWrong.1: More chunks means more cost and more noise. Retrieve wide, but send few.
ifWrong.2: Context windows hold far more. The problem is cost and focus, not a hard limit.
ifWrong.3: Models often miss facts in the middle of long context, and you pay for every token.

questions.title: Count, don't search
questions.prompt: A user asks, "How many refunds did we issue last week?" What should the system do?
options: Route it to a SQL query on the orders data
Search the refund policy docs and let the LLM estimate
Run hybrid search over tickets and count the matches
Ask the LLM directly; it has seen refund data before
questions.keyIdea: Route each question to the source that can answer it.
questions.why: Counting needs a database query. Vector search returns similar text, not totals.

ifWrong.1: Policy docs explain refunds; they don't count them. The LLM would guess.
ifWrong.2: Ticket matches aren't refunds, and top-k search never returns every row.
ifWrong.3: The model has never seen your data. It would make up a number.

questions.title: Ranked 37th
questions.prompt: The right chunk ranks 37th for a question, but only the top 5 go into the prompt. What's the best next step?
options: Re-rank the top 50 so the right chunk moves up
Re-chunk every document, since the chunk is missing from the index
Switch to a larger LLM so it can answer without that chunk
Lower the LLM temperature so it stops guessing the answer
questions.keyIdea: Found but ranked too low is a ranking problem.
questions.why: Search already found the chunk. A re-ranker scores the top candidates more carefully and moves it into the top 5.

ifWrong.1: It's in the index: it ranked 37th. Fix the ranking, not ingestion.
ifWrong.2: No model can use a chunk it never sees.
ifWrong.3: Temperature doesn't change which chunks reach the prompt.
